clue.text: Barista's warning police still?

definitions.meaning: a coffee server might caution that the cup is hot: read as two words
a photograph of a suspect taken by the police after arrest

explanation.surface: A coffee-shop worker shouts a warning, or perhaps tells the police to stay put.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer after its third letter and a barista's caution about a hot cup appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A police still is the custody photograph of an arrested person's face, taken front and side.

clue.text: Comic character who lacked a head for speaking

indicators.note: for speaking says the words that lacked a stand for are said out loud, giving the sound of a title

parts.note: lacked means missed, so lacked a is said 'missed a', which sounds like Mister, written MR
bean is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A comedian's creation who never had the wits to say much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missed a bean' (lacked a head) said quickly sounds like 'Mister Bean'; the title is entered in its short form MR. Mr Bean is Rowan Atkinson's near-silent British TV comic creation.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowan Atkinson's bumbling, almost wordless television figure is a famous comedic creation.

clue.text: Our crossword is a type one gets into

indicators.note: gets into tells us that the letter for one goes inside the word for a type

parts.note: a genus is a kind, class or type
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A boast that this very puzzle belongs to a category people get hooked on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our crossword' is the setter speaking for The Guardian, whose monthly prize puzzle bears this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Guardian runs a monthly prize puzzle under this title, so it is the paper's own crossword.

clue.text: Cleverly hide man and servant

indicators.note: cleverly suggests the letters of hide man and are ingeniously rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to conceal a man and his domestic help with some cunning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleverly' rearranges HIDEMANAND.
explanation.definitionFit: A female attendant or maid is a personal servant in old-fashioned terms.

clue.text: Milne's one was doubly good

parts.note: A. A. Milne's bouncy Pooh character is this big cat with its G (good) doubled

explanation.surface: A remark that a Winnie-the-Pooh character was twice as good.
explanation.walkthrough: Milne's character is Tigger: double the G (good) in the answer and his name appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Tigger in the Pooh stories is a striped big cat, the animal named here.

clue.text: Tendentious bid may be put forward after no end of hesitation

indicators.note: after places the word for put forward behind the shortened hesitation
no end of means the last letter of the word for hesitation is dropped

parts.note: doubt is hesitation or uncertainty
led means put forward or went in front

explanation.surface: A provocative proposal being advanced after a brief moment of uncertainty.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, an opponent may challenge a doubtful bid by doubling it, raising the stakes.
explanation.definitionFit: At contract bridge a contentious contract is challenged by an opponent's double, raising its scoring.

clue.text: Be tenured, potentially offering security

indicators.note: potentially hints the letters of be tenured could become something else when reordered

explanation.surface: Getting tenure as an academic might give you job security.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potentially' rearranges BETENURED; 'offering' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-term bond issued by a company is a financial security.

clue.text: With speech, makes pots

indicators.note: with speech means the word for makes is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: earns means makes, as in makes money

explanation.surface: Someone who earns a living by talking, and also turns out pots.
explanation.definitionFit: Large vases or vessels, as for ashes or tea, are pots.

clue.text: Vikings used this pine club with a hole in it

parts.note: to pine is to long or yearn

indicators.note: with ... in it says the letter for a hole sits inside the club
in it is part of the instruction placing the hole inside the club

parts.note: a bat is a club used in sport
O looks like a hole

explanation.surface: Something Norse raiders used: a club of pine wood with a hole bored through it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like the timber but is the verb to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse raiders crossed the seas in their long, narrow oared warships.

clue.text: Fail to keep up in time? Wretched!

indicators.note: in places the reversed word for fail to keep within the time word

parts.note: a date is a point in time

indicators.note: up reverses the word in this down clue, read from the bottom

parts.note: to lose something is to fail to keep it

explanation.surface: Someone falling behind schedule cries out in misery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fail to keep up' reads as one phrase about lagging, but 'up' is the reversal signal, giving ESOL.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling miserable and forlorn, utterly cheerless, is a synonym of wretched.

clue.text: Land one, punching Hilary

indicators.note: punching has the letter for one forced into the surname

parts.note: Hilary Benn is a British Labour politician
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone lands a punch on a person named Hilary.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilary Benn is a British Labour politician, son of Tony Benn.
explanation.definitionFit: A West African nation is a land, a country.

clue.text: Be wildly excited putting pineapple to mouth

indicators.note: putting ... to says the fruit is set beside the mouth, after it
to completes putting one thing against another

parts.note: gob is British slang for the mouth
ananas is another name for the pineapple

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled to bits as they bite into a pineapple.
explanation.walkthrough: GOB is British slang for mouth; ANANAS is the pineapple's name in French and botany.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to become frenzied or crazy with excitement.

clue.text: As naval fighter, put on a shade of blue

indicators.note: put on places the other words after the article in this across clue

parts.note: qua is Latin for as, in the capacity of
a marine is a soldier serving with the navy

explanation.surface: Dressing up as a sailor-soldier in a blue uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' is the Latin-derived QUA (in the capacity of), not a simple link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale greenish-blue colour named after the gemstone is a hue in the blue family.

clue.text: Endless ring makes a measure of sound

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the word for ring is removed

parts.note: a bell is something that rings

explanation.surface: A never-ending ringing noise turns into a measurement of loudness.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten decibels make one of these units for comparing sound intensity.

clue.text: Show off injuries from high-speed transport

parts.note: to sport something is to show it off
scars are marks left by injuries

explanation.surface: Showing off the wounds from a crash in a fast vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast two-seater motors built for performance are rapid vehicles.

clue.text: The French please with a mixture of tulips and violas

indicators.note: a mixture of tells us to mix the letters of tulips and violas together

explanation.surface: A French gardener's polite request for a mixed bunch of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a mixture of' rearranges TULIPSVIOLAS; 'with' and 'and' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase is the polite request word used across the Channel.

clue.text: Bombs huge town all round: that makes things sticky

parts.note: V1s, written VIS with I for 1, were German flying bombs in WWII

indicators.note: all round has the city word wrapped about the outsize letters

parts.note: a city is a large town
OS is the abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: Bombs falling around a huge town leave everything gummed up.
explanation.walkthrough: V1s were the German flying bombs of the Second World War, here written with I for the figure 1.
explanation.definitionFit: Thickness or resistance to flow is the property giving a liquid its gluey quality.

clue.text: Visionary site laid out

indicators.note: out suggests the letters of site laid are put out of order

explanation.surface: A dreamer surveys a building plot that has been planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid out' looks like a planning phrase; 'out' rearranges SITELAID.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreamer pursuing lofty principles is a visionary, a person of high ideals.

clue.text: Quick look as soon as finished

parts.note: once means as soon as, as in once you arrive
over means finished or ended

explanation.surface: Taking a brief glance the moment a job is done.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapid inspection or brief survey is a quick glance at something.

clue.text: What Midas was given, extremely sensibly hidden, so long ago

indicators.note: hidden says the end letters are tucked inside the donkey's ears

parts.note: in myth King Midas was given the ears of an ass (a donkey) by Apollo

indicators.note: extremely takes the outermost letters of sensibly

explanation.surface: Midas's punishment, sensibly concealed, belongs to the distant past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes the ends of sensibly and 'hidden' tucks them into the donkey's ears; 'so' is a link. King Midas was given ass's ears by Apollo for preferring Pan's music.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial British phrase means an age, a very lengthy time stretching back.

clue.text: Rotter's love, great mistake

indicators.note: mistake tells us the letters are wrongly arranged, so shuffle them

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shown as O

explanation.surface: A cad's affection turns out to be a terrible error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistake' rearranges OGREAT. The answer is British slang for a contemptible person.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a scoundrel or worthless cad, much like a rotter.

clue.text: Fan of one of Europe's currencies almost pocketed each

indicators.note: pocketed has the shortened currency enclose the letters for each
almost drops the final letter of the currency

parts.note: the zloty is the currency of Poland

explanation.surface: An enthusiast for a European currency who has pocketed some of each.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims the zloty to ZLOT, which 'pocketed' wraps around EA.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanatical supporter or enthusiast is an ardent follower or devotee.

clue.text: Fear wife's stuck in casualty

indicators.note: stuck in puts the letter for wife inside the hospital department

parts.note: A and E, accident and emergency, is the British hospital casualty department

explanation.surface: Someone frightened because their wife is stuck in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Casualty, or A&E (accident and emergency), is the British hospital emergency department.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverential dread or wonder mixed with fright is a kind of fear.

clue.text: Solicit a few pounds for Audrey's husband

parts.note: to touch someone for money is to solicit a loan from them
a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: Asking for a bit of money on behalf of a woman's husband.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's As You Like It, the clown Touchstone weds the goatherd Audrey. A stone is a British weight of 14 lb.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's court jester in As You Like It marries the country girl Audrey.

clue.text: Country's pro-Labour slogan?

definitions.meaning: split as ..., a call for the Conservatives (Cons) to be thrown out

explanation.surface: A nation's political rallying cry in favour of the Labour party.
explanation.walkthrough: Con is short for Conservative, the party opposed to Labour in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A large river nation of central Africa is a country.

clue.text: In a cell, what carries information regularly from Miranda

definitions.text: In a cell, what carries information

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of Miranda, starting with the first

explanation.surface: Messages smuggled regularly from a woman named Miranda to a prison cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cell' suggests a prison but is biological here.
explanation.definitionFit: Messenger RNA carries genetic code from the DNA to the ribosomes in a living cell.

clue.text: Popular edition getting everything topsy-turvy

parts.note: in means popular or fashionable
a version is an edition of something

explanation.surface: A best-selling edition of a book turns the world upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning things upside down or reversing their order is the act of upending.

clue.text: Penny in old money chucked back by such a fool

indicators.note: chucked back tells us the whole lot is turned round and read backwards
in puts the letter for penny inside the old currency

parts.note: the lira was the Italian currency before the euro

explanation.surface: A dupe who tossed a penny back into a pile of old coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts P inside LIRA to give LIRPA; 'chucked back' reverses it. The fool is one fooled on the first day of the fourth month.
explanation.definitionFit: The victim of a prank on the first of the month is that month's fool.

clue.text: Commonly, money (apart from euro) is thin

indicators.note: apart from removes the letter for euro from the slang money

parts.note: the ready is a colloquial word for cash, so commonly flags the slang
E is the symbol for euro

explanation.surface: A complaint that ordinary cash, other than the euro, is scarce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The ready' is informal British for ready money; remove one E.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a fine strand of fibre, a weak, faint pulse or voice is described this way.

clue.text: As soon as clocked in at workplace, given a hearing

indicators.note: given a hearing means the phrase for at workplace is spoken out loud

parts.note: on site means at the place of work

explanation.surface: An employee clocking in at work and then facing a disciplinary hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clocked' looks like punching a time clock but is slang for seen; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To clock someone is British slang for spotting them, so the phrase means immediately upon seeing.
